title: Querying Counterfactuals on Tissue Graphs with Supervised Disentanglement
claim: Define a family of interventions on local neighborhoods, then show one model that separates intrinsic state from context to answer them.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, problem cartoons left and model diagram right
description: The figure has two halves split by a thin vertical line. On the left, titled 'Tissue Graph Counterfactuals', two rows show a focal cell v ringed in blue and surrounded by six gray neighbor nodes, each with a small bar chart. The top row is edge perturbation: arrows labeled 'perturb' lead to a graph where three neighbors turn red and are rewired from a pool P marked by a lightning bolt. The bottom row is node perturbation: the neighbors' bar charts are modified, marked by δ and starred u*. On the right, titled 'Cellina', expression x_v feeds a blue encoder q(z|x) to a latent z labeled 'intrinsic'. The neighborhood feeds a red encoder q(s|N(v)) to a latent s labeled 'extrinsic'. Gray trapezoid blocks C and D (a classifier and an adversary) sit above z. A purple decoder p(x|z,s) outputs reconstructed x-hat. A contrastive box at the bottom shows anchor, positive and negative points. The eye goes first to the red perturbed nodes on the left.
caption: Tissue graph counterfactuals and Cellina overview. (Left) Two interventions on a focal cell $v$ with neighbors $u$: edge perturbation rewires $v$'s neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(v)$ to a counterfactual neighbor pool $\mathcal{P}$, and node perturbation alters neighbor expression on a feature (gene) subset $S$. (Right) Cellina encodes intrinsic identity $z \sim q(z \mid x_v)$ and spatial representation $s$ from $v$'s local neighborhood, and decodes $p(x \mid z, s)$. Supervision anchors $z$ to cell type and removes spatial-domain information adversarially; Cellina-GAT additionally applies a contrastive loss on $s$.
abstract: Tissue graph counterfactuals ask what a cell would express if its spatial neighborhood were altered, a question central to predicting cell behavior in tissues. Existing methods, however, present only specific instances of such queries. In this work, we first formalize tissue graph counterfactuals as a class of spatial interventions that either rewire connections between cells (edge perturbation) or modify the expression of their neighbors (node perturbation). We then introduce Cellina, a framework that uses supervised disentanglement to decompose a cell's intrinsic state from its spatial context, using the latter as a conditioning input for in-silico perturbation predictions. Across benchmarks spanning over 2.5 million spatially-resolved cells in observational and interventional screens, Cellina outperforms both spatially-informed and non-spatial competitors in in-silico perturbations, while training as fast as non-spatial methods. Moreover, we show that Cellina reveals cancer subdomains with distinct signaling programs in an unsupervised manner and enables targeted neighbor perturbation simulations.
